national.title: Israel's president formally gives Eisenkot the first chance to form the next government
national.summary: At the ceremony in Jerusalem, Eisenkot said he wanted a leadership that people can trust, that will act in the interests of the public and that represents all parts of society.
national.body:
Melanie Lidman, Associated Press Melanie Lidman, Associated Press

Giovanna Dell'Orto, Associated Press Giovanna Dell'Orto, Associated Press

JERUSALEM, Israel (AP) — Israeli President Isaac Herzog gave opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot the first chance to form the next government on Sunday evening.

After the formal announcement, Eisenkot, who ran as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's main rival, now has to launch complicated negotiations with potential coalition partners. He has six weeks to form a government.

At the ceremony in Jerusalem, Eisenkot said he wanted a leadership that people can trust, that will act in the interests of the public and that represents all parts of society.

The Oct. 27 election gave neither Netanyahu's bloc nor Eisenkot a clear majority in parliament. Among the kingmakers — and most politically fraught potential allies — are the Arab-led parties. They made historic gains in the election and have been a target of Netanyahu and his allies.

Eisenkot said Sunday that the conditions for parties joining his governing coalition are support for Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, for its declaration of independence, for military or national service, and recognizing the Hamas militant group as a terrorist organization.

While the announcement doesn't guarantee that Eisenkot will be the next prime minister, Herzog's decision is another blow to Netanyahu, who lost his parliamentary majority in the election.

national.title: Trains collide in Egypt, killing at least 4 people and injuring dozens
national.summary: The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 32 miles south of Cairo, when a train traveling to the southwestern Fayoum province crashed into the rear of another train.
national.body: Two trains collided south of the Egyptian capital of Cairo, killing at least four people and injuring nearly 90 others, authorities said.The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 32 miles south of Cairo, when a train traveling to the southwestern Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the Transportation Ministry. One of the trains derailed, it said, but did not specify which.The Health Ministry said at least four people were killed and 88 others were wounded. The injured were taken to nearby hospitals for treatment, it said.A train driver was among those killed in the collision, the Health Ministry said.President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi said in a social media post he is following the aftermath of the train collision "with great concern and extend my deepest condolences to the families of those who lost their lives.""I have directed state agencies to provide the necessary medical care, promptly investigate the circumstances of the accident and hold accountable anyone found to have been negligent," he wrote.Emergency teams and cranes were dispatched to the scene to clear the wreckage and restore train services to their normal schedule as soon as possible, the Egyptian Railway Authority said.Last September, a train driver and his assistant were injured after two freight trains collided in the same district.Over the past decade, Egypt has poured billions of dollars into updating its transport infrastructure, including new highways and high-speed rail lines, but has yet to overhaul much of its ageing rail network.

national.title: With "Thrasher," Brandon Flowers returns home
national.summary: Smalltown Nephi, Utah, was where the musical sensibilities of Killers frontman Brandon Flowers started to take form, before finding success as a rock star in Las Vegas. Now his solo album, "Thrasher," is filled with country songs like those beloved by his dad.
national.body: The year was 2002, in Henderson, Nevada, and no one at the bar that night realized they were watching what would become one of the biggest bands in the world: The Killers. No one, that is, except maybe Brandon Flowers, who was barely 23 years old when The Killers shot to stardom with their first single, "Mr. Brightside," a story about being cheated on ripped from Flowers' own life, which became the anthem for a generation."I noticed early on, people would talk about the storytelling in Killers music, that they didn't always associate with young rock bands," Flowers said. "And I think that was when it first started to maybe dawn on me, where was I getting this from?"Where he was getting it from turns out is Nephi, Utah, an hour and a half south of Salt Lake. It has one stoplight, and feels about as far away from rock & roll stardom as you could get. The family moved there from Las Vegas when Flowers was eight. "It's funny to look at it now, to say it was a culture shock," he said. "It really was, even though I was just a kid. My unit was my family, but there was something in me that still really felt planted in Las Vegas, and felt like that was part of my identity, you know? And it was something that I always wanted to go back to."Flowers struggled to fit in, missing school to help his dad work on an apartment building, a family business. (His sister's name is still on the mailbox.) And to buy music in Nephi back then, he headed to the closest thing Nephi had to a record store: The Flying J Truck Stop. "They used to have these bins inside our Flying J that would just be full of cassettes, and you'd kind of mine through them," he said. "One particular treasure that I found was a Depeche Mode record there."Another formative location in town? The local golf course. "This is the bar of the town," said Flowers. "This is where people can congregate and play a sport they love, but they can also drink. And so, there's sort of a subculture of guys that played golf here a lot. national.body: Yemen's Houthis on Sunday claimed responsibility for an attack on the financial district of Riyadh, Saudi Arabia's capital city, which witnesses said caused damage to a skyscraper belonging to oil giant Aramco. The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis had said earlier Sunday that its air defenses intercepted two ballistic missiles and two cruise missiles targeting Riyadh and other regions. In a statement, Houthi military spokesperson Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said the Iran-backed group carried out four military operations using ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as drones. Saree said the Riyadh airport was targeted in addition to the financial center, Aramco oil storage tanks, and the eastern Saudi city of Abqaiq. He said the Houthis were responding to attacks in recent days on a village near Yemen's capital, Sanaa, and at a market in southwestern Yemen, which he said left dozens dead or wounded and blamed on Saudi Arabia. Aramco facilities and infrastructure have been repeatedly struck by the Houthis in recent months, with tankers, refineries, storage areas and the company headquarters all targeted by the group. "Aramco tower in KAFD has been targeted, that's the sure thing," one witness told AFP, referring to the King Abdullah Financial District. Two other witnesses confirmed seeing damage to the building. One witness in the area of the Aramco skyscraper told AFP they saw a projectile strike the building but they were unsure what type of projectile it was. The Saudi Energy Ministry said there were no casualties at the Aramco facility. AP/AFP

national.title: Jon Meacham on the midterms and America's "better angels"
national.summary: In last week's historic elections, voters were asked to weigh in on whether our nation will maintain the ideals of equality, dignity, fair play, and the rule of law; historian Jon Meacham says that Americans overwhelmingly answered, and democracy prevailed.
national.body: What does Tuesday's seismic election say about America today? Perspective from Pulitzer Prize-winning author and historian Jon Meacham:In his long retirement in Independence, Missouri, Harry Truman spent a great deal of time musing about democracy and history. "The country," he remarked, "has to awaken every now and then to the fact that the people are responsible for the government they get."This week an American electorate woke with a start, registering a protest of historic dimensions. From Maine to Kansas, the Democratic Party upended years of assumptions about what was thought to be the most static of political landscapes, producing victories that reminded everyone — Democrat, Republican, and Independent — of the raw and resonant power of the ballot.Democrats have now flipped over 40 House seats. Here are all the districts that changed control in the midtermsDemocracy is messy because we (you and I) are messy. The American Founders understood this. "If men were angels," James Madison wrote, "no government would be necessary"— and given that men are so self-evidently un-angelic, the American government was designed to check our passions and balance our failings. For a decade now, the issues of our own un-angelic moments have been profound: Is the United States a sustainable enterprise grounded in equality, dignity, fair play, and the rule of law? Are we a republic that respects elections that go the other way? Are we a country with politicians and partisans able to lose graciously, and win graciously?These questions transcend red and blue; they're bigger than any policy debate or tax rate. And for the moment, the people have answered them affirmatively and definitively. The verdict has been accepted. The people have been heard. Democracy has prevailed.The Greeks were right: character is destiny — and destiny in Greek can also be translated as "fate." And so, America's fate depends on our dispositions of heart and of mind, on our capacity not to fear but to hope, on our willingness to heed not our worst instincts, but the better angels of our nature.This much is clear: Those better angels had a good week, because democracy had a good week. No matter your party, that's good for America, and Americans. Story produced by Robert Marston. Editor: Jason Schmidt. national.title: Judi Dench on an actor's life
national.summary: A film producer once told Judi Dench she had "everything wrong with her face." One Oscar and a Damehood later, she's had the last laugh. The actress, now 91, talks about her new memoir, "Is It Too Late to Make a Run for It?"
national.body: Judi Dench has made a career out of delivering just the right words, such as ait ("It's an island in a river"). During a game of Bananagrams with a friend, we saw the 91-year-old is still very much in command. "Don't expect any vowels, because I've got them all," she laughed.Although she can barely see the letters. "It's tricky if you're playing with an almost-blind person," she said. Her eyesight is almost gone, robbed by macular degeneration, but there's no diminishing Dame Judi Dench. She got her start on stage in 1957 as Ophelia in "Hamlet" at London's Old Vic Theatre. Her first starring role in film came 40 years later, in "Mrs. Brown." But her loyalties are clear. "Oh, theater, theater, theater, theater," Dench said.Asked what she loves so much about the theater, she replied, "I love the fact of a group of people trying to get it better every night, whereas in film, they say 'Cut,' and you can't make it better."A meeting with a movie producer early on was not encouraging: "'I'm sorry,' he said, 'you have every single thing wrong with your face.' So I said, 'Fine,' and I walked out and back to the glorious Old Vic."She says that criticism didn't get to her: "No, because I didn't want to do films. But it must have stayed with me, and, I mean, I suppose my insides have dealt with it."Her face would become one of the best-known in cinema. She has been nominated for eight Academy Awards, winning an Oscar for her portrayal of Queen Elizabeth I in "Shakespeare in Love"; and she's appeared in eight James Bond films as M, the steely MI6 boss, originally opposite Pierce Brosnan."Pierce came to lunch not long ago," Dench said. "When he got to the front door, what I'd forgotten was that I have a doormat which says, 'I've been expecting you, Mr. Bond…' He liked that. I think he thought I'd put it there for the occasion!"What did they talk about? "Oh, everything, everything, of how frightened we were doing the first one together."Why frightened of shooting a Bond film? "Well, the responsibility of the part," she said. national.title: Russell Brand to learn sentence after being found guilty of rape and sexual assault
national.summary: Comedian Brand faces a "significant" prison sentence, which a London court judge is set to hand down on Monday.
national.body:
Comedian and actor Russell Brand leaves Southwark Crown Court in London, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. Alastair Grant/AP hide caption

Comedian Russell Brand faces a "significant" prison sentence, which a London court judge is set to hand down on Monday.

On Thursday the one-time MTV host turned Christian and spiritual influencer was found guilty on three counts of sexual assault and one of rape, after a four-week trial that garnered massive media attention.

Brand had denied all charges and said he never had sex without consent.

Law From comedian to convicted rapist: What to know about Russell Brand After the jury handed down the verdict, Judge Joel Bennathan told Brand, 51, that he faced a "significant custodial term."

Danny Shaw, a crime commentator and former BBC correspondent, posted on X that while the maximum sentence for rape in the UK is life, 10 years is the average sentence, and Brand was likely to receive between four to 13 years of prison time.

The trial examined seven historic charges against Brand, brought forward by six different women. He was found guilty on four of the charges: for raping a woman who'd been to one of his comedy shows in 2009, and sexually assaulting three others between 2004 and 2009. The locations of the sexual assaults were a bar, radio station and TV studio. Brand was also found not guilty of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

Brand's lawyer asked the judge on Thursday to grant his client bail so that he could spend the weekend with his three children, which the judge denied. Instead the one-time celebrity darling spent his first weekend in a prison cell in London.

national.body: Poland began two days of national mourning on Sunday, a day after a 24-year-old man with far-right views opened fire in a busy central square in Krakow, killing six people and wounding 15 others.The attack, which Poland's defense minister described as an "act of terror," happened in Main Square, a major tourist hub in the heart of Krakow's Old Town.The alleged shooter, a Polish man, was shot and wounded by police.The prosecutors said on Sunday they started an investigation for murder and attempted murder of numerous people, including police officers, with the act "constituting a terrorist offense."Four women and two men were killed in the Main Square shooting. Three of the women and one of the men were Polish, Krzysztof Jan Klęczar, the Malopolska regional governor, said on Sunday. A man from the U.K. and a woman from an unidentified foreign country were also among the dead.The bodies of three people — the assailant's sister, mother and father — were found at the man's house in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, a city about 93 miles northeast of Krakow. They likely died from gunshot wounds, authorities said.Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said the suspect holds "very radical" and "ultranationalistic" views."Everything indicates that he was fascinated by far-right ideologies," Kierwiński said at a news conference.The two police officers who stopped the gunman, in actions authorities hailed as heroic, remain in hospital. One of them is still in a coma while the other woke up from a coma, Klęczar said. Officials launched an appeal for blood donations for the benefit of the most seriously wounded officer."If it weren't for the efficient and selfless intervention of these two young men, the number of victims could have been significantly higher," Klęczar said.He said the assailant's father owned over 10 guns legally and that the attacker also owned guns. Local officials in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski said they seized seven weapons from the family home, bringing the total number recovered to 11, including four found in the possession of the man in Krakow or in his car.The suspect is also in critical condition after undergoing multiple surgeries. national.title: The SS United States and her final destination
national.summary: She was the fastest ocean liner in history. But the jet age took the SS United States out of service, and she wound up docked in Philadelphia for nearly 30 years. Now, she's scheduled to be scuttled off Florida, to become the world's largest artificial reef.
national.body: Even with her paint peeling and rivers of rust, the queen of the North Atlantic – five city blocks long, 12 stories high – still strikes quite a pose in the setting sun. The SS United States quickly became the fastest ocean liner in history. On her maiden voyage back in 1952, she reached speeds topping more than 40 miles an hour – a record for a transatlantic crossing that's never been broken.But she was elegant, too – stately and refined. During her nearly two decades in service, she carried four U.S. presidents, countless celebrities, and tens of thousands of happy voyagers. But what was once glamorous and spacious, the jet age did away with. Speed won out over starry nights at sea. By 1969, the SS United States was withdrawn from service, and that's what gets us back to her currently forlorn state. She wound up in Philadelphia, where for almost 30 years she sat with only spiders and sunbeams booking passage. But she was still impossible to ignore."She still casts a spell; there's something about her," said Susan Gibbs, president of a non-profit called the SS United States Conservancy. "She has always been this unabashedly American symbol that brings so many people together."Gibbs knows every inch of this ship. Her grandfather, William Francis Gibbs, designed the SS United States, with the U.S. military helping to foot the bill – a floating investment that could be converted in less than 24 hours into a troop ship to transport an entire division. "It may not seem that way now, but back then she was the space shuttle of her age," Gibbs said. Only her bones are left, however – her once-grand staircase is bare; the indoor salt-water swimming pool is now just a ghostly abyss; the dance floor is still here, but nothing else.And yet, there was still enough that Gibbs was determined to save. There were all kinds of ideas – museums, restaurants, event spaces – but no takers.Our one-time flagship seemed headed for the scrap heap. Until that is, one man had a wild idea: return the SS United States back to the Atlantic, not to sail, but to sink – sending her to the bottom of the sea where nature, instead of the wrecking ball, will take its course. At least six people were killed and more than a dozen others injured when a gunman suspected to have ties to the far-right opened fire in central Krakow, the second largest city in Poland.

Three bodies were found at his home when it was searched by police. Here is everything we know so far.

The attack began shortly before 15:00 local time (14:00 GMT) in Krakow's Main Market Square, the bustling central point of the city which is popular with tourists.

Police said a man drove into the square before beginning to fire "at random people from his car".

Footage shows scenes of panic as people fled, with the sound of gunfire clearly heard.

A passing tram was shot at during the apparently random attack, shattering windows but no passengers were injured.

Armed officers raced to the scene and engaged in a gunfight with the suspect, who was shot within three minutes of the attack beginning, preventing a further massacre, officials said.

A 25-year-old man who was arrested remains in hospital after having surgery for a gunshot wound. The Krakow branch of the National Public Prosecutor's Office in Poland has announced an investigation into what constitutes "a terrorist offence".

national.body: Veterinarian Dr. Troy Hudnall enjoyed an active practice in Missouri. But in 2022, during an intense delivery of a calf, he felt a sharp pain, and heard a strange sound: "A snap or a pop, snap's probably the best way to describe it," he said.Herniated discs and a pinched nerve in his neck caused numbness and severe muscle loss in Hudnall's right hand: "The first thing that I really remember is, I couldn't click my mouse on my computer. national.title: UFC's Dana White says he will meet with Trump Monday over offer to be White House press secretary
national.summary: President Donald Trump said Saturday that he has offered the job of White House press secretary to his friend and UFC boss Dana White.
national.body:
FILE - President Donald Trump waves alongside Dana White, president and CEO of UFC, as they arrive for the UFC Freedom 250 on the South Lawn of the White House, June 14, 2026, in Washington. Mark Schiefelbein/AP hide caption

WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. — President Donald Trump said Saturday that he has offered the job of White House press secretary to his friend and UFC boss Dana White, an announcement unconventional even for the norm-busting president. White said Saturday that he plans to meet with Trump on Monday at the White House.

Trump, while he was at his golf club in Florida, posted on social media that he made the offer to "the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior" to become the Republican president's chief spokesperson.

Sports UFC boss Dana White says 'never again' to another White House fight night White, who was in London on Saturday for a boxing event, was asked at a news conference about Trump's post and responded by saying that he planned to fly to Washington right after and meet with Trump on Monday.

When asked how he would balance the job with the current positions he has in the fighting world, White seemed confused by the question and then said, "Yeah, I got a lot of jobs already."

He declined to say what conversations he'd had with Trump but said, "I'm sure I'll have more to talk about after that."

Before the news conference, the UFC head shared an image of Trump's post on Instagram, along with an image of himself standing behind the podium in the White House press briefing room with the words "On to the next chapter."

The White House and a spokesperson for the UFC did not respond Saturday to messages inquiring about the Truth Social post.

national.body: A New York City Department of Education employee is facing a murder charge in the stabbing death of a 28-year-old woman last week in Brooklyn, authorities announced Saturday. Katie Suarez was stabbed while jogging along the Shore Parkway greenway in Brooklyn on the evening of Oct. 30. Her father found Suarez injured along the path. She was rushed to the hospital with a stab wound to her neck but ultimately died from her injuries. On Saturday, the NYPD said it had arrested 27-year-old Sayed Mohassib, of Bath Beach, Brooklyn. Mohassib is charged with second-degree murder, tampering with physical evidence, and criminal possession of a weapon. Mohassib, wearing flip flops and a red jacket, did not answer any questions when police walked him out of the 62nd Precinct Saturday afternoon. The circumstances leading to Suarez's killing were not immediately clear. It also wasn't immediately clear what led police to Mohassib. NYPD sources say he made statements claiming he "blacked out" and doesn't remember hurting anyone. Mohassib was taken in for questioning Friday, police sources said, but they have not yet shared details on how they tied him to the crime. Police sources say Mohassib and Suarez both attended Brooklyn College at the same time, but right now there's no evidence that they knew each other. The suspect is an employee of the New York City Department of Education. Police sources say he worked at Public School 200 in Brooklyn, and that he was also a member of the NYPD in field training in the Bronx from October to November 2022. national.summary: Saudi Arabia, which leads a coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen, has not commented.
national.body:
Media linked to the Houthi movement in Yemen say at least 33 people, including women and children, have been killed in air strikes by Saudi Arabia.

There has been no comment from the Saudi-led coalition backing the internationally recognised government in Yemen.

Live video footage on Al Masirah - a television station run by the Houthis - has shown rescuers pulling bodies out of the rubble of several buildings in al-Shariyah, a town to the east of the capital, Sanaa.

The bodies of young children can be seen among those dug out from the ruins.

The television station has also shown a number of injured people being carried on stretchers to hospital.

Saba news agency, which is also run by the Houthis, said the attack was carried out by Saudi Arabia on Saturday. It added that 39 people had been injured.

The Saudis have led a coalition that has been fighting the Houthis for more than a decade in support of Yemen's internationally recognised government.

The war in Yemen had been dormant for several years but reignited as a result of the Iran war.

national.title: The Trump coalition is shattered - what will Republicans do now?
national.summary: Republicans can stick with Trumpism or chart a new path, writes BBC Washington correspondent Daniel Bush.
national.body:
Republicans are in soul-searching mode after the coalition that powered Donald Trump to three straight presidential nominations imploded in spectacular fashion in the 2026 midterms.

The stunning election defeat immediately raised questions about the party's future post-Trump.

But there are no easy answers as Republicans face the choice of doubling down on Trumpism or trying to chart a new path forward in his final years in office.

The depth of the problem was captured by outgoing Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who called the midterms "close to an extinction-level event for Republicans".

Others struck a more optimistic tone. Vice-President JD Vance, who blamed the midterm results on public anger over the war with Iran, argued the party could turn things around. Nevertheless Vance acknowledged the fallout will be messy.

"There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why," Vance said.

The wide range of reactions on the right highlights deep fault lines in the party that formed around Trump's improbable rise to the presidency in 2016 and never really went away.

It's too early to tell which faction will win. But while Republicans are still licking their wounds, the intraparty battle Vance predicted is already under way.

national.title: Germans wrestle with what to do with Hitler's destroyed Eagle's Nest retreat
national.summary: While some believe the site should be partially or completely rebuilt, others want it abandoned and all memory of its Nazi past forgotten.
national.body:
Perched on a ridge high up in the spectacular scenery of the German Alps lie the burned-out ruins of a mountain house called The Eagle's Nest, which is now at the heart of an intense debate about Germany's Nazi past.

Known in German as Kehlsteinhaus, the retreat was built by the Nazis in 1938, and frequented by Adolf Hitler and other high-ranking Nazis and their guests. After World War Two it was classified as a historical monument recalling the Nazi era.

Last month it was gutted by fire in a suspected arson attack, and some believe it should be completely destroyed, the site returned to nature and all memory of its Nazi past forgotten.

But others want it either partially or completely rebuilt, wary of the risk of turning it into a site for Neo-Nazi pilgrimage at a time when Germany is witnessing the resurgence of the far-right.

Germany has an "everlasting responsibility to communicate, to deal with our Nazi past", said Isabel Heinemann, professor of contemporary history at Munich's Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität (LMU).

But rebuilding the site completely, she warned, would mean putting "highly ideologised or highly ideological architecture" back in place.

Before it was burned down during the evening of 23 October, the Eagle's Nest had been a popular tourist attraction, owned by the state of Bavaria and operating for many years as a restaurant.

Visitors would take a bus and then ride the original brass and mirror-panelled lift through the mountain to the Kehlsteinhaus to savour the magnificent views above the town of Berchtesgaden.

national.summary: It was unclear how genuine the president's offer was, although White later said he would travel to Washington for them to meet.

US President Donald Trump has asked Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) boss Dana White to be White House press secretary, in a social media post.

"Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "Dana, please take the job!"

It was unclear whether the president's public job offer was genuine, although White said later on Saturday: "I'm going to meet with him, we have a meeting on Monday".

The vacancy for White House press secretary has been open since mid-October, when Katie Zacharia quit less than five days into the job.

Trump's post on Saturday afternoon comes after his fellow Republicans were routed in the US midterm elections, losing their congressional majorities.

The president called White "a violent Fighter and Warrior" and asked that he bring a number of high-profile UFC fighters with him on the job "even though some are not from our Country".

"We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left," Trump wrote, alongside photos of the six fighters.

Following Trump's post, White posted an Instagram photo of himself behind the lectern in the White House press briefing room.

national.title: Homelessness in the U.S. saw its largest drop in more than a decade last year
national.summary: Homelessness declined after years of record-high levels but it still remains at nearly 700,000. The Trump administration and homeless advocacy groups cite different reasons for the drop.
national.body:
People line up along temporary tents to partake in a free Thanksgiving meal provided by the Union Rescue Mission as the Los Angeles Skid Row district annual feast hosts thousands of homeless and others in need, in downtown Los Angeles on Nov. 24, 2022. Damian Dovarganes/AP hide caption

After years of increasing to record-high levels , the homeless population in the U.S. dropped more than 6% in 2025. That amounts to roughly 49,000 fewer people without housing. It's the second year in a row that homelessness has declined, with a smaller drop in 2024.

"President Trump's actions to secure the border, get criminal illegals off our streets, and restore safety to our communities drove a historic decrease in homelessness," Housing and Urban Development Secretary Scott Turner said in a press release announcing the results of an annual count in communities around the country. The agency had not yet posted a detailed report.

A second independent analysis based on the same count, but commissioned by the advocacy group National Alliance to End Homelessness, found a similar decline but credited different reasons for it.

"It's good news that more people are getting housed, and that the programs that are funded by Congress are working," said CEO Ann Oliva.

Both analyses find there's still nearly 700,000 people in the U.S. living in shelters or on the streets, significantly more than before the COVID-19 pandemic.

Only on NPR A homeless man was charged with a felony for camping. He's one of the first The Trump administration cited its changes in immigration policy as a key factor in the decline. During the Biden administration, New York, Chicago, Boston and Denver all saw a surge in asylum seekers who turned up at homeless shelters. "That's also the four cities that have driven half of the drop most recently," said Devon Kurtz, Public Safety Policy Director at the Cicero Institute, an administration ally on homelessness policy.

Kurtz also pointed to declines in cities like San Francisco, which is moving to support more sober-living options , housing that bans drugs and alcohol. But critics say that can send more people back to the street if they relapse, which is common.

national.title: What is Diwali, the Festival of Lights, and how is it celebrated?
national.summary: The festival follows the Hindu lunar calendar, typically falling in late October or early November. This year, Diwali falls on Nov. 8.
national.body:
Deepa Bharath, Associated Press Deepa Bharath, Associated Press

Diwali is the most important festival of the year in India, particularly for Hindus, and widely marked by prayers, family gatherings and the lighting of fireworks.

More than one billion people across faiths celebrate it in the world's most populous nation and its diaspora.

The name Diwali comes from "Deepavali," meaning "a row of lights." Celebrants place rows of traditional clay oil lamps outside their homes to symbolize the victory of light over darkness and knowledge over ignorance.

The festival follows the Hindu lunar calendar, typically falling in late October or early November. This year, Diwali falls on Nov. 8.

While Diwali is a major religious festival for Hindus, it is also observed by Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists. Its origin stories vary by region but share a theme: the victory of good over evil.

In southern India, Diwali celebrates Lord Krishna's victory over the demon Naraka, who is said to have imprisoned women and tormented his subjects. In northern India, it honors the triumphant return of Lord Rama, his wife, Sita, and his brother, Lakshmana, after 14 years of exile in the forest.

national.title: Israel's president tasks opposition leader Eisenkot with forming government
national.summary: Neither PM Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc nor that of his rival secured a majority in last week's election.
national.body:
Israel's president says he will task opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot with forming a new coalition government.

Isaac Herzog has been holding talks with political parties after neither Eisenkot's bloc nor that of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu secured a majority in Israel's parliament, known as the Knesset, following last week's election.

Eisenkot will now have 28 days to try to form a new administration, with a potential 14-day extension.

"Now is the time to form a national emergency government. I will do everything to ensure we are worthy," the former military chief wrote on X.

No political party in Israel has ever won an outright majority, meaning all governments have been coalitions.

Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies won 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, while Eisenkot's centrist Yashar party and three other Jewish opposition parties in his bloc won 48.

Two Arab-led alliances, the United Arab List and the Joint List, together won an unprecedented 19 seats following a surge in turnout among Arab voters.

That positions them as potential kingmakers. However, all but one of the Jewish parties pledged before the polls not to work with them to form a government.

local.title: Nature’s fall colors not as appealing on ground
local.summary: It seems weird that November has arrived and so many leaves are still clinging to the trees. It also might seem weird that someone (like me) would look forward to their falling because it’s fun to rake them up into big piles and stuff them in bags. But this essay is not about the therapeutic […]
local.body:
It seems weird that November has arrived and so many leaves are still clinging to the trees. It also might seem weird that someone (like me) would look forward to their falling because it's fun to rake them up into big piles and stuff them in bags. But this essay is not about the therapeutic value of wielding a stick with a large claw on the end to swipe at and gather up a zillion multi-colored dead pieces of tree matter. It's about other odds and ends having to do with the fall season.

Recently, I watched a girl and her mother in Washington Park. It was a breezy day, and the girl, I suppose 10 years old, was dancing in circles under the trees, her arms outstretched, head thrown back as she welcomed clusters of leaves floating down from the maples. Her mother was recording the scene on her phone. I was witnessing something very good, very lovely.

But people are fickle. They ooh and aah about how colorful the trees are. But when it comes time to deal with the fallout, their attitude changes. Awe and wonder are displaced by a sudden urgency to do battle, and lots of folks begin pulling out the big guns -- their monster leaf blowers! One neighbor, a registered leaf hater, owns a blower that seems bigger than himself, so big that he ought to put wheels on it to move it around the yard. When he fires it up, the roar is so extreme as to make birds from all over the neighborhood take flight. Squirrels plug their ears in panic, lose their balance and plummet from high branches.

I watched this neighbor recently as he finished blowing every last fragment of leaf into the street until his lawn looked like a dull greenish-brown rug. Then suddenly there was a sound from the north, kind of like a kettle drum roll. It was the god of autumn, seeming to say, "Silly mortal! Repent!" And in one mighty breath, all the leaves were blown back into the man's yard!

Fall sometimes leads to a philosophical debate about ownership and responsibility. Outside in the yard, neighbors pretend to be friendly toward one another, saying things like, "isn't it a lovely fall day" or "winter will be here before you know it." But behind closed doors someone's hissing, "all those damn leaves are coming from THEIR tree, and it should be THEIR responsibility!"

In the past, my yard raking has produced about 20 large leaf bags each year. I would empty them at the transfer site on Lucas avenue, saving all the bags to use in following years. But for some reason, I'm no longer allowed to do that. Instead, I was instructed to empty my bags on the terrace in front of my house, and the city would pick them up in a couple days. So later that day I built a two-feet high leaf ridge the length of the sidewalk in front of my house. A week went by, and the ridge was still there. But then one night, the wind picked up, and in the morning all the leaves were miraculously gone! Well, not really gone, just re-distributed in my yard and the neighbors'.

local.title: Christian music strikes the right chord
local.summary: I heard it as a teenager. I said it as a parent and a teacher. You may have too. “How can you listen to that crap? It’s terrible. Do you even know what the lyrics are saying? That’s not music.” And you may have given or received the same response. “I don’t listen to the […]
local.body:
I heard it as a teenager. I said it as a parent and a teacher. You may have too. "How can you listen to that crap? It's terrible. Do you even know what the lyrics are saying? That's not music." And you may have given or received the same response. "I don't listen to the words. I just like the beat." Or something to the effect of, "The artist is just expressing their emotions or making social commentary." Or " I don't mind the profanity, that's just the way that they talk."

I never actively looked for Christian-themed music until I taught my son's Faith Formation class more than a decade ago. There were Christian songs that I enjoyed listening to after stumbling upon them as a boy, teenager or adult. Some of these songs I didn't even know were Christian themed until I closely examined the lyrics. "Kyrie" by Mister Mister is a perfect example. I am not sure that George Harrison's "My Sweet Lord" is truly Christian themed but I do remember thoroughly enjoying listening to Harrison's song being sung during mass at St. Anthony's in the early 70s. You have to be of a certain age to remember Sister Janet Mead's 1974 hit "The Lord's Prayer" or Norman Greenbaum's 1969 hit "Spirit in the Sky". I don't remember there being Christian radio stations when I was growing up but I was never pointed in that direction. I listened exclusively to Top 40 music when I was a kid and a young adult except when forced to listen to other styles of music.

I volunteered to teach my son's Faith Formation class because St. Anthony's could not find an instructor at the time. I soon found out that teaching Catholic Doctrine and the Christian Faith was a bit more difficult than teaching mathematics to kids. While it was challenging teaching Faith Formation, it was also very rewarding. Just like teaching mathematics, I have learned so much about Catholicism and my Christian faith by studying it in order to teach it to others.

One of the ways that I tried to engage youngsters learning about Jesus was through music. I had upbeat Christian music playing for my Sunday School students as they entered the classroom each week. I pointed out to them that no matter what genre of music you like, there are artists performing Christian songs in that genre. There is Christian Rock, Christian Rap, Christian Heavy Metal, Christian Pop and Christian Country music. I told my Sunday School students, if you like a certain style of music, find a Christian artist that performs it, listen and enjoy it. And if you're really not concerned with the lyrics then why not listen to a style of music that doesn't include messages about sex, violence, drugs and other vices? A positive message just might come to you as you enjoy the rhythm and the beat of your favorite style of music with a Christian theme.

local.body:
The operators of a veterans retreat in Bemus Point are fighting charges filed in August by the state Attorney General’s Office.

Attorney General Letitia James alleges Healing for Heroes – A Disabled Veteran’s Retreat and Wooded Oasis Inc. defrauded donors, billed itself as an outdoor retreat for disabled veterans and hosted limited retreats that served board members and their friends and family - essentially using the charity to fund their own vacations. An investigation by the Office of the Attorney General (OAG) found that the owners of Healing for Heroes’ 30-acre property, Board President Thomas Nelsen and Jennifer Milchanoski-Nelsen, board secretary and treasurer, rented out the property on Airbnb on at least 32 different occasions in 2024 and 2025, claiming all proceeds would go to their charity. Instead, the couple kept the $33,312.16 proceeds from the rentals for themselves. The Attorney General’s office investigation also found that almost half of the nearly $100,000 donated to the organization was spent on property maintenance and improvements, such as a bathroom renovation and a new deck for the property, as well as personal shopping, meals, vehicle repair and gas expenses for board members.

The Nelsens, through their attorney, are fighting back in court documents filed recently in state Supreme Court in Erie County.

“This case is a classic example of government overreach,” attorney Ryan K. Cummings of Hodgson Russ LLP in Buffalo wrote in his Memorandum in Opposition to the state’s petition. “The Attorney General’s office began with the headline it wanted for its election-season press release and created a story to support that headline. The AG’s story is a fiction based on assumptions, innuendo, and falsehoods. As a threshold matter, the petition is not supported by evidence in admissible form. It is built on attorney representations that are not made on personal knowledge. It relies on a series of documents that have not been authenticated or provided and in many instances those summaries are demonstrably wrong. Finally, the petition is predicated on two affirmations from the fall of 2025 by two individuals who were tangentially involved with Healing for Heroes – A Disabled Veteran’s Retreat and Wooded Oasis Inc., separated from the organization in May 2024 and February 2025, respectively, and who were unceremoniously cut off from the organization following dishonorable conduct. The AG’s house of cards collapses under the weight of these infirmities.”

local.title: Club hears history of artist Norman Rockwell
local.summary: Joyce Haines presented her paper on notable New Yorker, Norman Rockwell, at a recent meeting of the Fredonia Shakespeare Club, hosted by Ms. Lucille Richardson. Although Norman Perceval Rockwell was born in New York City in 1884, making him a Notable New Yorker, he moved to Vermont and later to Stoc
local.body:
Joyce Haines presented her paper on notable New Yorker, Norman Rockwell, at a recent meeting of the Fredonia Shakespeare Club, hosted by Ms. Lucille Richardson.

Although Norman Perceval Rockwell was born in New York City in 1884, making him a Notable New Yorker, he moved to Vermont and later to Stockbridge, Mass., where he delighted in a calm, idyllic location to work on his paintings and illustrations.

Rockwell loved to tell stories in pictures. He always considered the concept, clothes, props, postures, and profiles of his subject, then photographed them, made sketches, and produced the illustration. He used local people for his models. Haines showed an original cover from The Saturday Evening Post, published the month and year she was born, which was the cover of her baby book written by her mother.

In 1941 wartime, President Franklin D. Roosevelt gave a speech about the four freedoms of Americans to inspire everyone. Rockwell wanted to do something for the war effort, so he did paintings representing each of the four freedoms in 1943: Freedom of Speech, Freedom of Worship, Freedom from Want and Freedom from Fear. Signed prints were distributed in schools and libraries, and those raised over $130 billion in bonds at rallies for the war effort.

In the 1960s, Rockwell turned to something more serious, working on the painting Do unto Others as You Would Have Them Do unto You. Members viewed a short video narrated by Rockwell himself detailing the making of this painting.

In 1963, he left the Post, and began making covers for Look magazine, where he had more freedom without constraints. It was a time of civil rights and desegregation. He expressed his thoughts with his painting of The Problem We All Live With, a depiction of Ruby Bridges being accompanied by guards on her first day of attending a white school.

Rockwell, a heavy smoker, died on Nov. 8, 1978, of emphysema at the age of 84 in his Stockbridge home.

A pristine museum located on the grounds of a well-groomed 36-acre campus just outside the village of Stockbridge houses his legacy of an archive of reference photographs, business and fan correspondence, props, costumes, and other materials that reflect his personal and professional life. It is just of the border from New York State off the I-90 and is well worth a visit.

JAMESTOWN - Audubon Community Nature Center has two fun learning opportunities for kids happening soon.

November Camp is Wednesday, 9 a.m.-3 p.m., with reservations required by Monday at AudubonCNC.org/november-camp. Ages 4-12 can enjoy the school holiday outdoors, being active before the cold sets in. They can explore, play, climb, run, and learn about animals gathering and storing food and plants ready to spend the winter in a state of dormancy. Learning and play are the themes of the day! Children should dress for the weather, bring water, snacks, lunch, and extras of anything that might get wet. Space is limited.The fee is $48 children 4-12, $36 member children, with a $5 sibling discount.

Always the second Saturday, this month Little Explorers is on Nov. 14, 10-11:30 a.m. Space is limited and paid reservations are required by Thursday, November 12 at AudubonCNC.org/november-little-explorers. Three- to 8-year-olds and their favorite grown-ups will learn about "Fur, Feathers, and Scales," the different coverings on animals' bodies to help them survive. Explore and compare these and learn how each adaptation helps the animals find food and survive predators or the climate. Enjoy a nature lesson, walk, and craft if there is time. The fee is $12 adults, $9 Nature Center members and children ages 3-8.

Audubon Community Nature Center is located at 1600 Riverside Road, one-quarter mile east of Route 62 between Jamestown, N.Y., and Warren, Pa. You can visit the nearly 600-acre nature preserve, look in on the live birds of prey, enjoy the native tree arboretum and Nature Play Area, and hike the six miles of trails dawn until dusk daily for free.

The three-story Nature Center building houses interactive displays, live animals, the Ralph Simpson Bird Collection, the indoor Nature Play Area, and the Blue Heron Gift Shop. Visitors are welcome Mondays through Saturdays, 10 a.m.-4:30 p.m., and Sundays, 1-4:30 p.m. Nature Center members and SNAP/EBT and Arts Access cardholders have free building admission daily. Building admission is also free Sundays for non-Nature Center members.

To learn more about Audubon and its many programs, call (716) 569-2345, find Audubon Community Nature Center on Facebook or Instagram, or visit AudubonCNC.org. Check out AudubonCNC.org/about for a quick fly-by.

Audubon Community Nature Center builds and nurtures connections between people and nature by providing positive outdoor experiences, opportunities to learn about and understand the natural world, and knowledge to act in environmentally responsible ways.

Special connection always on display at Centaur Stride
local.summary: The bond between horse and human is built on trust, recognition, and a quiet kind of love. What makes an animal a service or therapy animal? Is it the training, the loyalty, the connection, or perhaps the special garments, paperwork, and fees that sometimes accompany that designation? While these th
local.body:
Horses and humans have a special connection at Centaur Stride.

The bond between horse and human is built on trust, recognition, and a quiet kind of love.

What makes an animal a service or therapy animal? Is it the training, the loyalty, the connection, or perhaps the special garments, paperwork, and fees that sometimes accompany that designation? While these things may define an animal’s role, they don’t necessarily explain what makes the relationship between an animal and a human so extraordinary.

From the cherished stuffed animal of childhood to the faithful companion who walks beside us later in life, animals offer comfort, companionship, reassurance, and something difficult to put into words: the feeling that we are not alone. When it comes to emotional well-being, the connection itself can speak louder than any certificate.

Anyone who has welcomed a dog home after an absence knows the excitement of that reunion. The wagging tail, dancing feet, and unmistakable joy remind us how deeply animals can recognize and value our presence. Similar reunions between people and animals raised in human care remind us that connection can endure even across time and distance.

Every human being needs to feel recognized, welcomed, valued, and loved. But what happens when a disability makes it difficult or impossible for someone to care for an animal independently? Can that person still experience the remarkable connection animals offer?

This is where therapy animals can make such a meaningful difference.

An animal’s ability to connect with someone doesn’t depend on being that person’s personal pet. Through appropriate training, compassionate handling, and consistent care, animals can develop trusting relationships with many different people. They become partners in shared experiences, offering encouragement, confidence, companionship, and a sense of accomplishment.

local.body: Five months after Buffalo Police Officer Marc Hurst was shot six times while responding to a domestic violence call, he celebrated a moment that once seemed far from certain: marrying his fiancée, Haley."I'm just so thankful, you know, that we are celebrating our marriage on Friday and my family and my fiancée is not mourning the loss of me," Hurst said in an interview earlier this week.Hurst was responding to a call about a violent domestic May 26 near Broadway and Sherman Street when he was shot."One officer shot. Every available to Sherman," a dispatcher could be heard saying over police radio.Hurst was struck six times and rushed to ECMC.One of Hurst's friends in the police department called Haley with the news."I was like, 'You need to tell me what's going on,'" Haley recalled. "And he said that Marc had been shot."At first, she didn't know how serious his injuries were."I was obviously freaking out, like, he's been shot everywhere," she said.Hurst remembers realizing that despite being shot multiple times, he was still breathing and able to think."I just remember, and I believe it's just from the Lord, this overwhelming peace," Hurst said.As he focused on getting out of the house, another thought crossed his mind: his upcoming wedding."I remember being down on the ground and focusing on getting out of the house that we were in, but also being like, 'You know what? local.body: New York Assembly Speaker Carl Heastie faces questions about how a political committee under his control spent more than $1 million on sports-related events, including luxury suites and tickets to games involving some of the state's most popular professional sports teams.An investigation by New York Focus found the Democratic Assembly Campaign Committee paid teams, stadiums and sports-related companies more than $1 million since Heastie became Assembly Speaker in 2015. The spending included events involving the New York Yankees, New York Mets, Buffalo Sabres, Madison Square Garden, Barclays Center and UBS Arena.Heastie, a well-known sports fan, attended a number of those events, including a Subway Series game at Citi Field, an NBA playoff matchup at Madison Square Garden and games at Yankee Stadium.The investigation raises questions about whether the events were primarily legitimate political fundraising activities or provided personal benefits to Heastie and other political figures.The Democratic Assembly Campaign Committee's housekeeping account can accept unlimited corporate donations. However, state law restricts how that money can be spent.Housekeeping funds are intended to pay for permanent party headquarters and staff, as well as ordinary party activities that are not specifically intended to promote individual candidates.Spending that money on fundraising for the committee is permitted, and financial disclosure documents frequently listed fundraising as the expense code for the sports-related expenditures.But New York Focus reporter Sam Mellins questioned whether fundraising was always the actual goal, especially considering the photos Heastie posted on social media, posing with sports stars, friends and colleagues."Was that the primary purpose of the events, or was it primarily for the personal benefit of the politicians and the political figures involved? entertainment.title: U2 Sound Revitalized on ‘Carnaval de Luz’
entertainment.summary: The rock legends return with a tightly focused album that stands as a counterargument to pop-culture doomsaying
entertainment.body:
In the 1988 documentary Rattle and Hum , B.B. King chats with Bono , then 27. The bluesman reflects on his station in life: “[People] say, ‘There he is, a 62-year-old — and what is he trying to do?'”

It’s a question that U2 ‘s members may have asked themselves as they worked on Carnaval de Luz , their 16th full-length and first album of original music in nearly a decade. They were teens when the group formed in Dublin half a century ago, in their thirties when their art-damaged rock started to “fuck up the mainstream,” middle-aged when they reinvented themselves with “Beautiful Day,” and old enough to know better when they brute-forced Songs of Innocence onto your iPhone. Their resume boasts multiplatinum Number One hits, instant sellout tours, and household-name status. But now, here they are, sixtysomething years old — and what are they trying to do?

U2 show they’re nowhere close to a finish line on Carnaval de Luz , whose central theme seems to be “it’s not too late”: It’s not too late to party (“Go [Carnaval de Luz]”), not too late to find God (“Midnight Sunshine”), not too late for empathy (“Torn”), not too late to save a relationship (“If the World Is at War We Better Not Be”), not too late to save the world (“Street of Dreams”), and just plain not too late (“Can’t Stop Us Now”).

Each song is tight and punchy, memorable and melodic. The music is the opposite of the blues, as well as U2’s legend-making hits; it’s big, bright pop music with more silver linings than clouds and only a few minor keys. As always, U2 work best when they’re not trying too hard. The songs on Carnaval never recall “Pride (in the Name of Love),” or “One,” or “Stuck in a Moment,” but they do sound like U2 every time Bono opens his mouth and croons something profound (“Nobody is alone but nobody knows that,” on “La Reina”) as much as when he belts something a little corny (“Sing-a-ling the reggaeton,” also on “La Reina”). They sound like U2 whenever the Edge ‘s guitar echoes and chimes (“Street of Dreams,” the intro to “The Mirror Maker [Rosalía]”), when Adam Clayton ‘s bass stabs and undulates (“La Reina”), and when Larry Mullen Jr . plays a propulsive, march-like rhythm (“Can’t Stop Us Now”) — affectations that come to them naturally. Brandon “Bug” Hall has had several run-ins with the law since leaving Hollywood in 2020 to live off the grid in poverty.

Hall — best known for playing Alfalfa Switzer in the 1994 cult classic “The Little Rascals” — was arrested in Texas that June for allegedly huffing air duster cans .

At the time, a 911 caller claimed Hall may have overdosed after spotting him huffing by a hotel dumpster. When the police arrived, they discovered the “Get a Clue” actor in his hotel room surrounded by cans.

Upon investigation, Hall was arrested for misdemeanor possession for use to inhale or ingest a volatile chemical.

Then, in April 2026, Hall was arrested in Ohio and charged with failure to appear for a court date from December 2024.

Hall was previously given a traffic citation on Oct. 29, 2024, for not having liability insurance.

In 2022, Hall — who identifies as “a radical Catholic extremist” — was temporarily banned from X after he posted tweets in support of marital duty and corporal punishment of minors.

entertainment.summary: If you're having a bad day, these episodes of Friends will be there for you to always make you laugh and put a smile on your face.

Compared to contemporaries like "Seinfeld," "Will and Grace," and "Frasier," it's always talked about as a show that was great because it was romantic, cozy, and broadly wholesome — which means it rarely gets credit for how straight-up hilarious it can be.

Yes, we've ranked our favorite "Friends" episodes yet again, not based on how moving their stories are or how well they push the characters forward, but rather how much they made us laugh out loud. There's some overlap with the all-time greats; others are episodes with so-so storylines that are saved by absurd subplots. They're the episodes we quote the most, have imitated the most with our own friends, and are largely the reason why audiences keep coming back to this show two decades after it left the air. If you're having a hard day and need a reason to smile, these episodes will be there for you.

A common complaint about the later seasons of "Friends" is, to put it bluntly, that the show got dumb. "The One with Joey's New Brain" is proof that's not inherently a bad thing for a show — whether it's a hit sitcom or a long-running soap opera.

Joey (Matt LeBlanc) gets some unexpected good news when a writer on "Days of Our Lives" informs him that his character, Dr. Drake Ramoray, will finally be coming out of the coma he went into in "The One Where Dr. Ramoray Dies" (Season 2, Episode 18). The catch is that Drake's body will be piloted — via brain transplant — by Jessica Lockhart, a made-up, legendary "Days" character played by Cecilia Monroe (Susan Sarandon). It's the show leaning hard on its semiparodical use of the NBC soap, with Cecilia overcoming her hurt feelings enough to mentor Joey to become the next great soap diva.

The simple B-plot is just as, if not more, effective. It leads to a terrible live performance of "Celebration" by Kool & the Gang from Ross (David Schwimmer), which visibly breaks Jennifer Aniston. She and co-star Lisa Kudrow have described it as one of their favorite scenes in the entire series.

Strangely, the episode that seemingly killed Ross and Rachel's relationship once and for all was also a laugh-heavy half hour of TV. Their romance is equally sweet, chaotic, and toxic for the majority of the show's run, but "The One with the Jellyfish" shows why that balance is so perfect for layering character development and comedy on top of one another.

entertainment.title: Jodie Sweetin Had $190 in Her Bank Account Before Filming Fuller House
entertainment.summary: Jodie Sweetin is shedding light on her past financial struggles. The Full House alum shared she fell on tough times before signing on for the sitcom’s 2016 reboot Fuller House, revealing she only...
entertainment.body:
Jodie Sweetin is shedding light on her past financial struggles.

The Full House alum shared she fell on tough times before signing on for the sitcom’s 2016 reboot Fuller House , revealing she only had about $190 to her name at the time.

“I had to borrow money the first week I was working on Fuller House , and I [skittered] into my first paycheck with like $190 in my bank account,” Sweetin recalled on a recent episode of the We’re Still Here, Babe podcast. “And nobody that I worked with knew that.”

Since Full House wrapped in 1995, Sweetin—who played Stephanie Tanner on the show—has been open about the cycle of partying and drug use she fell into after cameras stopped rolling. And it wasn’t long until she found herself with “no money,” which forced her to find a job outside of the spotlight to make ends meet.

“I didn’t have [an] ego about it,” Sweetin explained. “I didn’t care that I was, quote, unquote, working a normal job. I think other people again were like, ‘What are you doing here?’ And I was like, ‘Paying my bills. Kids don’t pay for themselves.’”

That’s why Sweetin—who shares daughters Zoie , 18, with ex-husband Cody Herpin and Beatrix , 16, with ex Morty Coyle —spent her days as a logistics coordinator at a treatment center in Los Angeles before returning to TV.

At the time, she lived in a one-and-a-half-bedroom apartment with her two kids, sharing she made $2,200 a month.

But in knowing what she does now, Sweetin says she wouldn’t trade her less-than-glamorous chapter for the world.

entertainment.title: Before Star Trek, Leonard Nimoy Appeared In A Popular Action Series As 8 Different Characters
entertainment.summary: In a true testament to his versatility as an actor, Leonard Nimoy played several different roles on this series, including that of a mustachioed villain.
entertainment.body:
Airing from 1958 to 1961, "Sea Hunt" starred Lloyd Bridges as scuba diver Mike Nelson, and the rest of the cast largely depended upon a revolving door of guest actors. Fortunately for Nimoy, "Sea Hunt" was willing to give the same actors different assignments, and he did his part to put a different spin on each performance. "I'd do one with a mustache; I would do one with a hat," he recalled to The Television Academy in 2000. "I could do an accent of various kinds, so I was useful." Nimoy also had great respect for Bridges, which made him an ideal person to rehire.

Some of Nimoy's roles were so small that they didn't even make the credits — during Season 2, he played a revolutionary student in one episode, and a liquid explosives thief in another. Others, however, were more substantial. In his first appearance, a 1958 episode called "The Shipwreck," Nimoy played Vince, a character stranded in the middle of the ocean on Nelson's lifeboat. It's a meatier role compared to some of Nimoy's other guest spots, like when he had fewer than five lines on "Matinee Theater" with Vincent Price .

Ziv Television For his second "Sea Hunt" appearance, Leonard Nimoy returned three episodes later as Tyler, a mustached man accused of murdering his wife during a scuba expedition. After his guilt is uncovered, a dramatic underwater wrestling match unfolds as Tyler tries to escape justice. During the show's second season, Nimoy returned (sans mustache) as Johnny Brand, a fisherman who starts taking diving lessons from Mike Nelson as part of a jailbreak scheme. In his next appearance, Nimoy's Jerry Wiley is a diver accidentally poisoned by an underwater wreck.

After the two background character episodes, Nimoy returned for Episodes 28 and 30 in Season 3 of the show. First, he played a sneaky saboteur in a straw hat who rigged up underwater explosives amid political turmoil. His final "Sea Hunt" role is a similar theme with a twist: Nimoy plays Indio Ramirez, a diver learning underwater demolition.

While Nimoy went on to play a mix of other guest roles across a variety of genres, "Sea Hunt" was a particularly good opportunity. One old contract shows he got a day rate of $125, which was a nice increase compared to an $80 flat fee for two days on another show. Multiple appearances were sometimes bundled together for a rate of $500 for two episodes, and the job security was crucial. "For a period of time they called me every three or four weeks, which sustained us," he informed The Television Academy decades later. "I had two kids, and I needed work."

entertainment.title: Future-Prog Foursome Polyphia Want to Freak You Out on Their New Album
entertainment.summary: Next-gen guitar shredders Tim Henson and Scott LePage on why their band got heavy and scary while staying weird on ‘Be Not Afraid’
entertainment.body:
If the term “post-rock” wasn’t already taken, it would be a perfect descriptor for the fractured, future-warped music of Polyphia , a largely instrumental foursome who take virtuosic guitar music into places that would melt older shredders’ minds. Even as fleet-fingered guitarists Tim Henson and Scott LePage keep pushing guitar technique forward, they’ve evinced minimal interest in carrying on any rock lineage, and are instead obsessed with bringing influences from pop, EDM, hip-hop, and video-game soundtracks into a ferocious live-band context. Older-school shredder Steve Vai paid his respects with a guest appearance on their last album, 2022’s Remember That You Will Die , and longtime Kanye West producer Mike Dean is one of their heroes and a fan in his own right — he had Henson and LePage open for him at a rare live show in 2024.

The band’s just-released new album, Be Not Afraid , is as quirky as ever, but it has some of their heaviest songs yet, with more overt nods to metal than usual. Henson and LePage hopped on a Zoom with Rolling Stone to dig into their latest influences, the making of the album, and how they get their rhythm section (bassist Clay Gober and drummer Clay Aeschliman — yes, they’re both named Clay) to sound inhuman. They also weigh in on the rise of fellow instrumental oddballs Angine de la Poitrine.

Tim was way ahead of a huge trend in guitar playing — ditching physical, tube amps for digital modeling. Scott, are you post-amp as well? Scott LePage: Yeah. When we were kids, digital amp modeling was kind of coming up, and we were like, “Huh, we can buy this one thing and not have a bunch of other things that are massive and heavy and expensive.” It almost wasn’t even an option to have a bunch of amps as a 16-year-old kid. So having the fake version of all the things is kind of sick. My dad got me this DigiTech thing. It was an effects thingy that had some amp modeling in it, but the main thing was [the 2009 software plug-in] POD Farm. Some of those models still hold up now. We still use it from time to time — that Angel P-Ball one that they have, Big Bottom, that’s a classic and everyone knows that one.
